fixes.explanation: You got it, baker. Adoni-zedek, king of Jerusalem, sends word to Hoham, Piram, Japhia and Debir. His message says, “Come up and help me. We will attack Gibeon…” (Joshua 10:4). He's alarmed, so he does what you do when the group chat is the only plan you've got. He calls in every king he can reach.

I get it, alarmed people sometimes head for the exits. But the text never has this king leave Jerusalem. It says he sends word to four kings and asks them to come up and help him attack Gibeon (Joshua 10:3-4). Adoni-zedek isn't running from this problem, he's recruiting for it.

Pharaoh, Egypt's king, never shows up anywhere in this passage. The men of Gibeon send word to Joshua in the camp at Gilgal. They say, “Do not abandon your servants. Come quickly and save us!” (Joshua 10:6). When you need help fast, you call the one name on your list, and Gibeon's list says Joshua.

True, baker. Verse 7 says Joshua and his whole army, including all the mighty men of valor, came from Gilgal. Not a small team and not a few volunteers. When Gibeon calls, the whole army moves, and I think that's one loud parade of sandals.

Close, because the mighty men are in the story. But verse 7 says Joshua came with his whole army, including all the mighty men of valor. And the LORD's words in verse 8 aren't about who to bring at all. He says, “Do not be afraid of them…” (Joshua 10:8).

Chains would be a neat way to stop an army, but the text doesn't mention them. It says the LORD threw them into confusion before Israel (Joshua 10:10). That confusion is what the text gives us, and it's the word that belongs in the blank.

An angel going before the camp does show up elsewhere in the Bible, like in Exodus 14:19, but not in this passage. Verse 14 says what makes the day one of a kind: the LORD listened to the voice of a man. That man is Joshua, who had just called out to the sun and moon. The writer adds that the LORD fought for Israel.
